title: Zašto bosanski?
theme: Orientation. what Bosnian is and who this course is for
reviewerNotes: Published for live preview. Orientation chapter. comparative notes intentional on Lesson 0 only.
storyBeat: Before Ana lands in Sarajevo, we pause for a clear map. What Bosnian is, where the name comes from, how it relates to neighboring standards, who speaks it, and who these lessons are for.

grammar.title: This course teaches Bosnian. Latin script only
grammar.explanation: From Lesson 1 you will see and type Bosnian in the Latin alphabet (with letters like č, ć, š, ž, đ). Official Bosnian can also appear in Cyrillic, but this course never teaches or displays Cyrillic. One path, one script, less noise.

grammar.title: Book 1 teaches phrases rather than full grammar tables
grammar.explanation: Bosnian grammar is real and complicated. Cases, endings, and long verb charts can overwhelm beginners. Book 1 does not teach that full system. You learn ready phrases and present-tense chunks you can say today. Order coffee, ask the time, introduce yourself, stay polite. Grammar labels appear only to help you notice a useful pattern. Full paradigms and past-tense storytelling wait for Book 2.

examples.english: I am Ana. (say the whole line)

grammar.title: Close neighbors, separate standards
grammar.explanation: Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian share a common South Slavic dialect base (Štokavian) and are largely mutually intelligible. They are separate standard languages with their own norms, preferred words, and cultural identities. This course teaches standard Bosnian as used in Bosnia and Herzegovina. After today, we will not add “also in Croatian…” sidebars. we stay in Bosnian.

culture.title: A language of a whole country. not only one city
culture.body: Bosnian (bosanski) is a South Slavic language and one of the official languages of Bosnia and Herzegovina (Bosna i Hercegovina / BiH). The name comes from the historic region of Bosnia. People have used forms of this name for the speech of the land for centuries. In the 1990s, after independence, Bosnian was codified as a modern standard with spelling and grammar guides, alongside Croatian and Serbian as official languages of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Speakers often understand one another across those standards, but names matter. Calling the language Bosnian honors the country’s identity and the forms you will hear from the mountains to the Neretva, in Mostar, Travnik, Banja Luka, Sarajevo, and beyond. Book 1 starts Ana’s story in Sarajevo, but Lesson 0 is about the whole map.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A. What is Bosnian, and where does the name come from?
lessonBlocks.body: Bosnian is the standard language taught and used as bosanski jezik in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The word bosanski comes from Bosna, the name of the region and the river Bosna, plus a Slavic adjective ending that roughly means of Bosnia. So the language name is tied to place rather than to a single invented brand. Standard Bosnian is built on the widespread Štokavian dialect shared with neighboring standards. The area sat at a crossroads of Slavic speech, Ottoman administration, and Austro-Hungarian schooling. That history left everyday Bosnian with familiar Slavic words plus older loanwords from Turkish, Arabic, and Persian that feel at home in café talk, food talk, and everyday politeness. You do not need the full history to start. You need one clear label. You are learning Bosnian.
tips: Say bosanski jezik aloud once. It means Bosnian language.
The name points to Bosnia (Bosna), the place.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B. Why Bosnian is not “just Croatian or Serbian,” and who speaks it
lessonBlocks.body: People often ask whether Bosnian is the same as Croatian or Serbian. The honest short answer is that speakers can usually understand each other, because the standards grew from the same dialect family. The honest longer answer is that they are not the same course, the same classroom label, or the same cultural home. Differences show up in preferred vocabulary, some spelling and sound habits, script choices in public life, and identity above all. Bosnian is an official language of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is spoken by Bosniaks and by many other people across the country, and it is also spoken in diaspora communities worldwide. Neighbors may call their own standards Croatian or Serbian. Mutual understanding does not erase those names. This book teaches Bosnian forms used in everyday life in Bosnia and Herzegovina. From Lesson 1 we will not train you to compare three columns of vocabulary. We will train you to sound at home saying zdravo in Sarajevo.
tips: Mutual understanding is not the same as identical language identity.
After Lesson 0, stay Bosnian-focused. There are no comparative sidebars.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson C. Why learn Bosnian, and who these lessons are for
lessonBlocks.body: Why Bosnian? Because you care about this place and these people. You may visit Bosnia and Herzegovina for a short stay, begin an expat year, have family or partners with roots here, reclaim a home language from diaspora, or refuse a vague Balkans label. Book 1 is a tourist and early-expat survival path. Order food, find your way, talk about weather and rooms, meet people politely, and stay in the present tense. Bosnian grammar (cases, endings, long charts) is rich and complicated, so Book 1 does not teach that full system yet. You learn ready phrases and present-tense chunks you can use this week. This course is for absolute beginners and false beginners who read English. It fits adults and older teens who can spend about an hour a day with Latin-script Bosnian only. It is not a linguistics degree, a three-language comparative grammar, a Cyrillic course, or an A2 storytelling course. Past-tense stories and deeper grammar wait for Book 2. Lesson 0 is your map. Lesson 1 is your first step onto the stone streets of Baščaršija.
tips: If you can read this page in English, you are in the right audience.
Expect phrases you can say rather than case tables to memorize.
Plan about 35 minutes today, then about 60 minutes from Lesson 1.

funFacts.title: Etymology in one line
funFacts.body: Bosanski is basically “Bosnian / of Bosnia”. The language name is anchored in the place name Bosna.

funFacts.title: Official rather than obscure
funFacts.body: Bosnian is an official language of Bosnia and Herzegovina, used in schools, media, and daily life. Not a dialect label invented for tourists.

funFacts.title: Mutual understanding, separate classrooms
funFacts.body: A traveler who learns Bosnian will understand a lot next door. And still be studying a named standard with its own books, news, and pride.

funFacts.title: Why we skip Cyrillic here
funFacts.body: Less split attention. Master Latin Bosnian first. You can explore other scripts later if you want.

funFacts.title: Why we skip the big grammar table
funFacts.body: Bosnian has cases and endings that can overwhelm beginners. Book 1 keeps you speaking with short, reusable lines. You will see grammar labels, but you learn phrases first. The big tables come later in Book 2.

questions.question: How should you think about Bosnian vs Croatian/Serbian for this course?

Closely related, largely mutually intelligible standards. we teach Bosnian forms and stay Bosnian-focused after Lesson 0

civicContext.title: Two schools under one roof
civicContext.body: In parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, children from different ethnic communities still attend school under a segregated model often called two schools under one roof. Students may share one building while using separate entrances, teachers, classrooms, and history lessons. International monitors have documented the practice for years as everyday discrimination in education. The result is that children in the same town can grow up learning different versions of the past inside the same walls.
